framework.name: C3 Framework for Social Studies State Standards
framework.source: https://www.socialstudies.org/standards/c3 (NCSS, 2013; indicator wording is the school's own; codes are the C3 indicators where one applies)

strands.strand: Dimension 1: Developing Questions and Planning Inquiries
strands.subStrand: Dimension 1: Developing Questions and Planning Inquiries

objectives.description: Choose the kinds of sources that will best answer a question about an early civilization.
Explain what historians mean by prehistory and history, and use a timeline to order early human development.
Explain how geography and climate shaped the growth of Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley and China.
Use maps and population data to describe how early societies met their needs for food and water.
Analyze the causes and effects of the agricultural revolution on early societies.
Compare the political, religious and social systems of the first river-valley civilizations.
Describe how Greek ideas about citizenship, philosophy and democracy developed, and how people of the time saw them.
Analyze the causes and effects of Alexander's conquests and the Hellenistic world.
Describe how the Roman Republic became an empire and the effects on the people it ruled.
Analyze the causes and effects of the rise and decline of the Roman and Han empires.
Describe the Maurya and Gupta empires of India and their contributions to mathematics and science.
Compare the beliefs and practices of Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism and Christianity and explain how each spread.

strands.strand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence
strands.subStrand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence

objectives.description: Gather information about the Silk Road and Indian Ocean trade from several primary and secondary sources.
Identify what an ancient inscription, a coin and a chronicle can and cannot show as evidence.

strands.strand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence
strands.subStrand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence

objectives.description: Combine evidence from several sources to support a claim about how ideas spread along trade routes.
Use evidence from several sources to argue why one classical empire lasted longer than another.

strands.strand: Dimension 4: Communicating Conclusions and Taking Informed Action
strands.subStrand: Dimension 4: Communicating Conclusions and Taking Informed Action

objectives.description: Construct an explanation of a turning point in the ancient world with precise vocabulary.
Build an argument about which factor most shaped a classical civilization, supported by specific evidence.

strands.strand: Dimension 1: Developing Questions and Planning Inquiries
strands.subStrand: Dimension 1: Developing Questions and Planning Inquiries

objectives.description: Frame a question about colonial America and decide which documents will help answer it.
Explain how geography and motives shaped the settlement of the Chesapeake, New England and the Middle Colonies.
Describe how Native nations, Europeans and enslaved Africans experienced colonial America.
Analyze the causes and effects of the growth of slavery and the Atlantic trade.
Trace the changes in colonial government and the ideas of the Enlightenment that shaped them.
Analyze the causes of the French and Indian War and its effects on the colonies and Britain.
Separate the long-term causes of the American Revolution from the events that set it off.
Compare the Declaration of Independence with a historian's account of why the colonists broke with Britain.
Describe the experiences and choices of patriots, loyalists, women, and enslaved and free Black people in the war.
Use several sources to argue why the Americans won the Revolutionary War.
Explain how the Articles of Confederation were organized and why they were replaced.
Explain how the Constitution created a government with limits and the compromises that made it possible.
Describe how Federalists and Anti-Federalists reasoned about the new government.
Explain why the Bill of Rights was added and how it protects individual liberties.
Analyze how the early republic changed under Washington, Adams and Jefferson.
Identify the limits of a letter, a newspaper and a pamphlet as evidence of public opinion in the 1790s.

strands.strand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence
strands.subStrand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence

objectives.description: Evaluate the credibility of primary sources from the founding era.

strands.strand: Dimension 4: Communicating Conclusions and Taking Informed Action
strands.subStrand: Dimension 4: Communicating Conclusions and Taking Informed Action

objectives.description: Build an evidence-based argument about whether the Constitution was a compromise or a victory for one side.
Distinguish the powers of local, state, tribal and national governments and give an example of each.
Explain why governments exist and compare forms of government such as democracy, monarchy and authoritarian rule.
Explain the major ideas that shaped the American founding, such as natural rights, consent of the governed and the social contract.
Describe how the Declaration, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution each answered the question of how to govern.
Explain how the Constitution sets up separation of powers and checks and balances, and how that has changed.
Describe federalism and how powers are divided and shared between the nation and the states.
Explain the formal and informal ways the Constitution changes, including amendments and judicial interpretation.
Describe the structure, powers and leadership of Congress and how a bill becomes law.
Analyze the powers and the limits of the presidency and the executive branch.
Describe how the federal courts work and the role of judicial review in Marbury v. Madison.
Analyze the role of citizens in the political system, including voting, serving and protesting.
Analyze how personal interests and perspectives affect how people use civil rights and liberties.
Examine the First Amendment freedoms and landmark Supreme Court cases about speech and religion.
Explain due process and the rights of the accused in the Fourth through Eighth Amendments.
Explain how the Fourteenth Amendment has been used to apply the Bill of Rights to the states.

strands.strand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence
strands.subStrand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence

objectives.description: Evaluate a news report and a government source on the same issue for credibility and bias.

strands.strand: Dimension 4: Communicating Conclusions and Taking Informed Action
strands.subStrand: Dimension 4: Communicating Conclusions and Taking Informed Action

objectives.description: Present an argument on a public issue to an audience, with attention to counterarguments.
Assess options for individual and group action on a local issue and take one step.
Explain scarcity, opportunity cost and trade-offs, and apply them to a personal decision.
Analyze how incentives influence the choices of people and the costs and benefits for different groups.
Use marginal benefits and marginal costs to argue for or against a solution to an economic problem.
Describe the three basic economic questions and compare market, command and mixed economies.
Describe the factors of production and show how a production possibilities curve shows trade-offs.
Explain how consumers decide what to buy and build and interpret a demand curve.
Explain how producers decide what to sell and build and interpret a supply curve.
Show how supply and demand set a market price and what happens at shortages and surpluses.
Explain what shifts supply and demand and predict the effect of a change on price and quantity.
Analyze how incentives affect what a market system produces and distributes.
Describe elasticity of demand and why it matters to a seller.
Compare perfect competition, monopoly and oligopoly and their effects on consumers.
Explain the role of the government in markets, including taxes, regulation and externalities.
Describe how business owners choose a form of business and what profit is.
Describe how labor markets set wages and how education and skills affect earnings.
Use a budget, a loan and compound interest to make a savings plan.

strands.strand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence
strands.subStrand: Dimension 3: Evaluating Sources and Using Evidence

objectives.description: Gather and compare data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and other sources on a question about the economy.

strands.strand: Dimension 4: Communicating Conclusions and Taking Informed Action
strands.subStrand: Dimension 4: Communicating Conclusions and Taking Informed Action

objectives.description: Build an argument about an economic policy using data and economic reasoning.
